passage: Before the uniformed police forces that appeared in many large cities during the nineteenth century, the keeping of order was a patchwork. Night watchmen walked fixed rounds, parish constables served unpaid and often unwillingly, and private thief-takers recovered stolen goods for a fee, sometimes from the very thieves they claimed to pursue. What was new about the reformed police was not that they caught criminals more efficiently. It was the claim that a salaried, disciplined body of officers, visible on the street at all hours, could prevent offences from occurring at all. The patrol, rather than the arrest, was meant to be the core of the institution.

This founding idea has an awkward property: its successes cannot be seen. A burglary that does not happen leaves no record, and a street that stays quiet because an officer passed through it twenty minutes earlier looks exactly like a street that would have stayed quiet anyway. The arrest, by contrast, is countable. It produces a name, a charge and a figure that can be reported upward and compared from one year to the next. Over time, institutions tend to drift toward what they can count, and police forces have been no exception. Officers come to be judged by how many people they detain, and the quiet beat, which was supposed to be the whole point, comes to look like idleness.

It would be too simple to conclude that the preventive ideal was therefore an illusion. Critics sometimes point out that putting more officers on the street does not reliably reduce recorded crime, and they are right to be sceptical of large claims about deterrence. But the patrol was never only about deterrence. A visible and predictable presence tells residents that someone is responsible for the shared space of the street, and that sense of being looked after shapes whether people walk out at night, whether they report what they see, and whether they regard the police as theirs or as an occupying force. These effects are as hard to count as the burglary that did not happen, but they are not imaginary.

The deeper lesson concerns what happens when a public institution is measured by its most legible output rather than by its purpose. A force that rewards arrests will produce arrests, and it may do so in ways that erode the trust on which prevention depends. Recovering the original idea does not mean abandoning measurement; it means admitting that some of the most important things a police force does will show up, if at all, only as an absence.

passage: For much of the twentieth century, average raw scores on intelligence tests rose steadily in country after country, so steadily that the tests had to be renormed at intervals to keep the average at one hundred. The rise, which came to be called the Flynn effect after the researcher who did most to document it, presents an awkward dilemma. If the tests measure intelligence and the gains are real, then our grandparents, scored against today's norms, would have been of strikingly low intelligence, and a substantial share of them would have fallen in a range we now associate with serious intellectual difficulty. That conclusion is absurd on its face, and it is worth saying why: those generations ran farms, businesses and governments, and nobody who knew them found them obtuse. If instead the gains are an artefact of testing, it is hard to see why the artefact should be so large, so persistent and so widespread.

The way out begins with a closer look at where the gains occurred. They were not spread evenly across the tests. They were largest on tasks that ask for abstract classification and for the detection of patterns in unfamiliar material, and much smaller on tasks that draw on stored knowledge, such as vocabulary and arithmetic. Consider a person asked what a spade and a pair of shears have in common. She can answer that both are tools, or that one is used to dig the flower bed and the other to trim the hedge around it. The first answer earns credit; the second does not. Yet the second is not stupid. It reflects a habit of thinking about things in terms of their practical relations, a habit well suited to a life in which what matters about a spade is whether it will break the ground before the rain comes.

On this reading, the twentieth century did not make people more intelligent in some general sense; it trained a particular style of thought. Mass schooling, work that deals in symbols rather than objects, and a culture saturated with categories and hypotheticals rewarded the habit of setting aside what things are for and attending to what kind of thing they are. The tests, built by people who had that habit, measured it well. Nor is the spread of the habit a trivial change, since it is precisely the habit that a world of written rules, formal classifications and hypothetical planning keeps demanding of the people who live in it. The gains are therefore real, since the habit genuinely spread, but they are not gains in a single underlying power that would make the average person of today a match for the most gifted minds of a century ago.

This resolution is attractive, but it has a price that is not always acknowledged. If scores on the most abstract tests reflect habits cultivated by a particular kind of society, then the tests cannot be quite what they were often taken to be, a culture-free measure of raw capacity. They remain good predictors of success in schools and workplaces, but partly because those institutions demand the very habits the tests detect. It does not follow that the tests are worthless, or that differences in scores within a generation mean nothing; among people educated in broadly similar ways, scores can still capture real differences in how well they reason. What does follow is that comparisons across generations, and across societies with very different patterns of schooling and work, need to be interpreted with far more caution than a single number invites.

passage: Any decision whose costs and benefits are spread over time requires some way of comparing what happens now with what happens later, and the standard device is the discount rate. A benefit expected in a year is counted as worth somewhat less than the same benefit today; one expected in ten years, less again; and so on, at a compounding rate. Within a single human life, and over horizons of a few decades, the practice is largely uncontroversial. Its consequences become startling only when the horizon stretches across centuries. At a rate of five per cent a year, a harm that will occur two hundred years from now is valued today at a tiny fraction of one per cent of its full size, so that a policy which spared our descendants a catastrophe would barely register against even modest present costs. Whether we owe the future anything substantial thus turns, in practice, on a number that is usually set by technical convention.

It helps to separate the reasons that have been given for discounting, because they do not stand or fall together. One is pure time preference: the view that well-being simply matters less the later it occurs. Another appeals to growth. If future people will be considerably richer than we are, then a given sum of money, or a given quantity of goods, will make less difference to their lives than it would to ours, much as a rupee means less to a wealthy person than to a poor one. A third appeals to uncertainty: the further away an outcome, the less sure we can be that it will happen at all, or that there will be anyone for it to happen to.

Pure time preference is the weakest of these, at least when it is applied across generations. A person who prefers a pleasure today to a larger one next year may be imprudent, but the impatience is his own and so are its costs. To discount the well-being of people not yet born merely because they will be born later is a different matter: it is to treat a position in time as a reason for counting someone's suffering as less, in just the way that it would be indefensible to count suffering as less because it occurs in a distant country. The growth argument is more respectable, because it does not deny the equal standing of future people; it says only that the same resources will do them less good. But it is respectable only on its own assumptions. It presupposes that the future will in fact be richer, which is precisely what is in doubt if the harm in question is severe enough to undermine prosperity, and it applies only to losses for which wealth can compensate. A flooded coastline or an extinct species is not made good by a larger economy, and to discount such losses at the rate at which consumption grows is to treat them as though they could be bought back.

The argument from uncertainty deserves more sympathy than critics of discounting usually allow it. It is reasonable to give some weight to the possibility that there will be no future people at all, and a small discount for that possibility is defensible. But the rate this argument supports is far lower than the rates commonly used, and it has nothing to say about harms we are confident will occur. What emerges from these distinctions is that the choice of a discount rate is not the technical matter it is often taken to be. Each component encodes a substantive view: about whether time itself diminishes moral standing, about how confident we are in continued growth, about which losses money can repair. A rate presented as a neutral parameter is, in effect, a verdict on what the present owes to the future, reached without the argument such a verdict requires.

passage: Whether insects can suffer is a question on which serious people disagree, and on which the evidence is likely to remain inconclusive for a long time. Their nervous systems are tiny and organised very differently from ours; some of their behaviour looks like nothing more than reflex, while some looks uncomfortably like the behaviour that, in a dog or a bird, we would take without hesitation as a sign of pain. Faced with this uncertainty, the usual response is to treat it as permission. If we cannot know that insects feel anything, the thought runs, we need not worry about how we treat them.

This inference is much weaker than it looks. Uncertainty about whether a being can suffer is not the same as confidence that it cannot, and in other contexts we do not treat it so. A builder who is unsure whether a house is occupied does not demolish it on the grounds that no one has proved anyone is inside. What uncertainty calls for is a weighing: the probability that harm is occurring, multiplied by how bad the harm would be and by how many beings it would affect. With insects, the last factor is overwhelming. The numbers involved in agriculture, pest control and the growing industry that farms insects for animal feed run to many billions, so that even a modest probability of sentience yields a large expected total of suffering.

The obvious objection is that this style of reasoning proves too much. If any probability of suffering above zero, multiplied by a sufficiently large number of beings, can generate an overriding moral demand, then we might find ourselves obliged to reorganise our lives around bacteria, or around the remote chance that plants feel pain. That objection has force against arguments resting on probabilities so small that they amount to mere logical possibility. It has much less force here. The case for insect sentience is not a bare possibility of the kind that could be raised for any organism; it rests on specific behavioural and physiological features that insects share with animals whose capacity for pain we already accept, even if they share them only partially.

What follows is not that insects should be accorded the same consideration as mammals, nor that every crushed ant is a tragedy. It is that where we deliberately bring insects into existence in vast numbers and kill them, as in insect farming, we should prefer methods of rearing and killing that would minimise suffering if suffering is present, provided the cost of doing so is modest. Precautions of this kind ask little of us. To refuse them on the grounds that sentience has not been proved is to mistake the absence of certainty for the presence of a licence.

passage: When a person pushes a door that should have been pulled, the usual verdict is that the person was careless, and the verdict is so automatic that we rarely notice how strange it is. A door has one job that involves its user, which is to tell an approaching hand what to do, and a door that sends the wrong message has failed at that job as surely as a door that sticks in its frame. Yet the failure is booked to the person, who apologises and blushes, while the door goes on misleading everyone who comes after.

The habit of blaming users has a simple source, which is that designers judge their objects from the inside. They know which way the door swings because they drew it, and they know which button on the oven sets the timer because they chose its position. What is obvious to someone who already knows the answer tells us very little about what an object communicates to someone meeting it for the first time, in a hurry, with a bag in one hand. A flat plate invites pushing and a vertical bar invites pulling, whatever the small sign above them says. When the hardware and the sign disagree, people follow the hardware, and they are not foolish to do so, since the shape of a thing is read faster than words are.

There is a practical cost to the blaming habit beyond the irritation it causes. Errors that are attributed to individuals are treated by asking individuals to try harder: more signs, more training, more warnings printed in red. Errors that are attributed to design are treated by changing the design, which removes the error for everyone at once. Imagine a hospital in which two different medicines are supplied in bottles of the same size and colour. If it blames the nurse who confuses them, it may discipline that nurse and still find the confusion repeated next year by someone else; if it makes the bottles look different, it removes the occasion for the mistake altogether.

This is not to say that every mistake is the designer's fault, or that objects can be made so clear that nobody ever misuses them. Some tasks are intrinsically demanding, and some carelessness is simply carelessness. But the sensible default runs the other way from the usual one. When many people make the same mistake with the same object, the repetition is itself a kind of evidence, and it points less at the people than at the thing they all share.

passage: Few episodes have shaken social psychology as much as the attempts, over roughly the past decade and a half, to repeat some of its best-known experiments. Among the findings that fared worst were studies of so-called behavioural priming, which reported that subtle exposure to an idea could shift what people did shortly afterwards: that reading words associated with old age made people walk more slowly down a corridor, for instance, or that being reminded of money made them less helpful. Such results were taught in lecture halls and retold in popular books. When larger and more carefully controlled attempts to reproduce several of them found effects much smaller than those first reported, or none that could be detected, the reaction within the field was bitter, and the debate quickly took on the character of a trial.

That framing has not served anyone well. It invites the question of who was dishonest, when the more troubling lesson is that dishonesty was largely unnecessary. A literature can come to look robust through practices that most of the people using them regarded as normal: running small studies, trying several reasonable ways of analysing the data and reporting the one that worked, and publishing successes while filing failures away. Each practice, taken alone, seems a minor licence. Together they make it likely that a field will accumulate striking positive results whether or not the underlying effects are real, and that the most surprising results, which are the most likely to be false, will also be the most celebrated.

It is important to be clear about what the failed replications do and do not show. They do not show that priming in general is an illusion. That encountering one word makes a related word easier to recognise a moment later is among the most reliable findings in the study of cognition, and nothing in the recent debate casts doubt on it. Nor does a failed repetition of a single study prove that the effect it sought is exactly zero; it shows that the effect, if it exists, is smaller or less dependable than the original report implied. The questions under dispute concern a particular, ambitious claim: that brief and incidental cues reliably steer complex social behaviour.

Defenders of that claim have often replied that social behaviour is sensitive to context, so that an effect obtained with one population, in one decade, with one set of materials, need not appear when any of these is changed. There is something to this. Human beings are not inert objects, and it would be strange if the meaning of a word list were identical across cultures and generations. But the reply has a cost that its proponents do not always acknowledge. The original studies were presented as revealing general features of human minds, not as local facts about particular groups of students. If the effects are so delicate that unknown features of a setting can abolish them, then those general claims were overstated, and an appeal to hidden moderators that is made only after a failure, and never specified in advance so that it could be tested, explains everything and therefore nothing.

The reforms that the episode prompted, such as registering hypotheses and analyses before collecting data and running studies large enough to detect modest effects, have costs of their own. Research becomes slower and more expensive, and fewer dazzling results will appear. That is the right trade. A science of social behaviour that publishes fewer surprises, each of which can bear weight, is worth more than one whose surprises must all be taken on trust.

passage: A familiar demonstration from the study of chess runs as follows. A position from a real game is shown for a few seconds and then removed, and players are asked to reconstruct it on an empty board. Strong players replace most of the pieces correctly, while novices manage only a handful, and the obvious conclusion is that strong players simply have better memories. The less obvious and more instructive part of the demonstration comes next. When the same pieces are scattered at random, in arrangements that could never arise in play, the masters' advantage largely disappears, and they do little better than beginners.

What the masters possess, then, is not a larger store for holding pieces but a different way of seeing them. Years of play have given them a vocabulary of familiar configurations, a castled king with its pawns in front, a bishop aimed down a long diagonal, and they take in a position as a few such units rather than as two dozen separate pieces. A novice looking at the same board sees wood on squares. The master sees a situation, and often, before any conscious calculation has begun, a sense of what the situation calls for.

Similar observations have been made in fields as different as radiology, birdwatching and the reading of geological maps, where experienced specialists frequently report knowing that something is wrong with an image within a second or two, before they can say what it is. The birdwatcher who names a distant species from the way it flies, long before any marking can be made out, is drawing on the same resource. It is tempting to describe this as intuition, as though it were a mysterious faculty standing apart from knowledge. It is better described as knowledge that has been absorbed into perception, so that it no longer needs to be consulted, because it shapes what is seen in the first place.

This view has practical consequences, though they are easily overstated. If expertise lies partly in the eye, it cannot be fully transmitted by rules and explanations; the learner has to look at a great many cases, with feedback, until the patterns become visible. But perception is not the whole of expertise. Masters still calculate, and careful specialists still check their first impressions, because a pattern that is recognised instantly can also be misrecognised instantly. The trained eye is fast and usually right within the territory that trained it, and that qualification matters: presented with a case unlike those it has learned from, its speed becomes a liability rather than an asset.

passage: The line between literary and genre fiction is usually drawn in terms of freedom. The literary novel, it is said, invents its own shape, while the crime novel, the romance and the tale of space travel arrive with their shapes already supplied: a body in the first chapter, an obstacle between the lovers, a voyage, a crisis and a return. To write in a genre is, on this account, to fill in a form someone else designed, and the best a genre writer can hope for is to fill it in with unusual skill. Critics who accept this account tend to praise a crime novel by saying that it rises above its genre, as though the genre were something to be escaped.

The account has the logic of constraint backwards. Nobody thinks a sonnet a lesser poem because its length and rhyme scheme were fixed before the poet began. We understand that the fixed form is what makes certain effects possible: a turn in the ninth line registers as a turn only because the reader knows where turns are expected. Genre conventions work in much the same way. A reader of detective stories knows that the culprit must be among the people introduced, that the clues must be fair, that a solution will come. These expectations are not a cage around the writer but an instrument she can play, and the slightest departure from them, a detective who is wrong, a solution that satisfies the law but not the reader, is felt with a precision no unconventional novel can command, because the unconventional novel has no settled expectation to depart from.

This is also why devoted readers of a genre are often its most exacting critics. Having read a hundred novels built on the same frame, they are alert to the smallest variation in it, much as a chess player who knows an opening thoroughly notices a single unusual move that a novice would pass over. Such readers can tell at once whether a twist is earned or merely borrowed, and they are rarely generous to a writer who mistakes one for the other. Their pleasure is not the passive pleasure of repetition but the active one of comparison.

None of this rescues every genre book. Conventions harden into formula when a writer treats them as a checklist to be completed rather than an expectation to be worked against, and a great deal of genre fiction is written in exactly this way. But the same is true of literary fiction, which has its own conventions, the quiet revelation in the final paragraph, the fractured chronology, the unnamed narrator, and its own writers who complete them dutifully. The useful distinction is not between books that have conventions and books that lack them, since none lack them, but between books that do something with their conventions and books that merely obey them.

passage: If biases are errors, it seems natural to suppose that teaching people about them should reduce them. Hence the many workshops in which managers, doctors and analysts are taken through a catalogue of the mind's failings, from anchoring to the sunk-cost fallacy, in the hope that knowing the names will help them avoid the traps. The hope is reasonable, and it is mostly disappointed. Participants usually leave such sessions able to define the biases and to spot them in descriptions of other people's reasoning. What they far less often do is reason differently when a fresh problem, dressed in unfamiliar clothes, arrives in their own work.

Part of the difficulty is that biases rarely announce themselves. A textbook problem about sunk costs is labelled, at least implicitly, by the chapter in which it appears; a real decision about whether to keep funding a struggling project comes with no such label, and with colleagues, budgets and reputations attached. Recognising a pattern in a tidy example is a different skill from noticing it in a messy situation, and teaching the first does not automatically produce the second. There is also a subtler obstacle. People readily accept that biases exist and readily see them at work in others, while judging their own conclusions to be the products of careful thought. Instruction can even sharpen this asymmetry, supplying a vocabulary for diagnosing colleagues without unsettling one's own sense of seeing clearly.

None of this shows that debiasing is hopeless. A few interventions built around repeated practice, varied examples and immediate feedback on one's own errors have produced improvements that outlasted the session, though how far they reach beyond the kinds of problem used in training remains uncertain. And there is a quieter strategy that sidesteps the question of individual reform altogether: changing the procedures within which decisions are made. A committee that collects independent estimates before discussion, or a review that requires someone to argue the case against a favoured plan, does not need its members to have become wiser. It builds the correction into the routine.

The contrast is instructive. Approaches that rely on informing the individual treat bias as a kind of ignorance, curable by knowledge. Approaches that redesign procedures treat it as a standing feature of minds working under ordinary conditions, to be managed rather than eliminated. The second view is less flattering, but it fits the evidence better, and it has the practical merit of not depending on each person's ability to catch themselves in the act.

passage: Collective security is one of those ideas that seem obviously right until one asks what they require. The principle is that an attack on any member of an international system is to be treated as an attack on all, so that every aggressor faces the combined strength of everyone else. Against this, the older practice of the balance of power looks cynical: states align against whichever power threatens to dominate, and they change sides as readily as the threat shifts, guided by interest rather than by any judgement about who is in the right.

The appeal of collective security lies in its impartiality, and so does its weakness. For the scheme to work, states must be willing to fight an aggressor regardless of who it is, which means fighting, if necessary, a friend, a major trading partner or a power whose goodwill they need elsewhere. They must also be willing to fight over places where they have no interest at all, because the principle admits no distinction between an attack that matters to them and one that does not. This is a great deal to ask of governments that answer to their own citizens, and the interwar experience suggests that, when the moment came, many would not pay the price. An organisation founded on the principle found its members ready to condemn aggression and reluctant to resist it.

The balance of power asks less and so delivers more reliably, at least within its narrower aims. It does not require states to care about aggression as such, only about the rise of a power that could threaten them, and so it draws on motives that governments actually have. But its reliability comes at a price. Because it attends only to the distribution of strength, it is indifferent to the fate of small states whose conquest does not upset the balance; it can tolerate, and has often arranged, the partition of a weak country as a way of keeping the strong ones satisfied. Stability is its aim, and justice enters only by accident.

The lesson is not that one principle should replace the other, but that each supplies what the other lacks. A norm against aggression, however imperfectly enforced, gives resistance to an expanding power a public justification and makes it easier to assemble allies who would hesitate to act on calculation alone. Balancing, in turn, supplies the motive that the norm cannot generate by itself. Orders that have lasted have usually combined the two, borrowing their legitimacy from the first and their enforcement from the second, and the mistake of the reformers who championed collective security was to imagine that legitimacy could do the work of both.

passage: Public debate about bureaucracy tends to oscillate between two complaints. One is that officials are rigid, applying rules mechanically to people whose circumstances the rules never anticipated. The other is that officials are arbitrary, treating similar applicants differently according to mood, prejudice or the length of the queue. The usual remedy for the second complaint is more rules: tighter eligibility criteria, standard forms, checklists that leave nothing to judgement. Each new scandal of favouritism produces another layer of instructions, and the layers accumulate. The remedy is seldom questioned, because it seems obvious that a rule applied uniformly is fairer than a person deciding as he pleases.

What this remedy overlooks is that the officials who deal directly with the public, the benefits clerk, the housing inspector, the teacher deciding which pupil needs extra help, cannot stop exercising judgement however detailed their instructions become. A rule says that an applicant must provide proof of address; it does not say how hard the clerk should look for an acceptable document when the applicant has been living with relatives. Moreover, such officials almost always have more cases than time. They must decide whose file to open first, whose story to probe and whose to accept, and these decisions shape outcomes as surely as any formal ruling. When rules are tightened, judgement does not disappear. It retreats into these less visible choices, where it is harder to observe and correct.

This is not to romanticise frontline discretion. The same latitude that allows a sympathetic clerk to find a way through for a desperate family allows an unsympathetic one to find reasons for delay, and there is ample reason to think that such latitude is not exercised evenly across applicants of different backgrounds. The case for discretion is not that officials can be trusted. It is that the choice is not between discretion and its absence, but between discretion that is acknowledged and discretion that is driven underground. Discretion of the first kind can be examined and improved; discretion of the second kind can only be suspected.

Seen this way, the task of administrative reform changes. Instead of writing rules ever more finely in the hope of closing every gap, an agency might record the informal decisions its staff actually make, review samples of cases to see how similar applicants fare, and give officials explicit guidance on the purposes their judgement should serve. None of these steps would remove judgement from the counter; they would make it something an agency can see, discuss and, where necessary, correct. Such measures concede what the rule-writer prefers to deny: that every system of rules ends, at its edges, in someone deciding.

passage: The quarrel between advocates of green growth and advocates of degrowth is usually staged as a dispute about a single empirical question: can economic output keep rising while the pressure it places on the planet falls? Green growth answers yes. Rich economies, it observes, have already shown that output and emissions can move apart, as electricity is generated from cleaner sources, heavy industry gives way to services, and the same goods are made with less material. Degrowth answers no, or not fast enough. Some of the apparent separation, it replies, reflects production moved abroad rather than pollution avoided; much of the rest is merely relative, a fall in emissions per unit of output that is swamped by the growth of output itself. On this view the only reliable way for rich countries to shrink their ecological footprint is to shrink their economies, or at least to stop enlarging them.

Both sides are right about something, and the way they frame the dispute obscures what it is really about. That emissions and output can diverge in absolute terms is no longer a mere hypothesis; it has happened in a number of countries, even after allowing for the carbon embodied in their imports. But the existence of absolute decoupling settles less than its champions suppose. The relevant question is not whether emissions can fall while output rises but whether they can fall fast enough, given how little more carbon the atmosphere can absorb before the damage becomes severe. A rate of decline that would be impressive in almost any other context may still be far too slow in this one. Equally, the degrowth case proves less than its champions suppose. That past decoupling has been too slow does not show that it must remain so; the pace of change in energy technology has repeatedly surprised forecasters, and the costs of some forms of clean power have fallen faster than most people expected a generation ago.

The deeper difficulty is that both camps take GDP as the variable of interest, one wishing to keep it rising and the other to see it fall. Yet GDP is neither the cause of environmental damage nor its cure. It is a sum of market transactions, some of which burn fuel and clear land and some of which, such as teaching, nursing or repairing, do very little of either. An economy could grow while its emissions fell sharply, if the growth came from activities of the second kind; it could shrink while its emissions rose, if a recession struck services harder than it struck heavy industry. To make the size of GDP the target, in either direction, is to aim at a proxy that is only loosely tied to the thing that matters.

A more productive stance would be indifference to growth as such. Policy would set limits directly on what does harm, through carbon prices, caps on extraction and the protection of land, and then let output rise or fall as it will within those limits. Such a stance asks something uncomfortable of each side. Advocates of green growth would have to accept that if the limits prove binding, slower growth may be the price, and that this would be not a failure of policy but a possible result of it. Advocates of degrowth would have to accept that if the limits are met while output rises, there is no further environmental case for shrinking the economy, whatever other reasons they may have for wanting a different kind of society. Neither concession is trivial, which may explain why the debate is so seldom conducted on these terms.

passage: When the sea threatens a coastal town, the first response is almost always to defend it. Walls are raised, beaches are replenished with sand pumped from offshore, and the line between land and water is held where it has always been. To propose instead that some places should be gradually abandoned sounds like defeatism, a confession that the town has been given up for lost. Yet the choice is rarely between holding the line and surrendering it. More often it is between retreat that is planned and retreat that is forced.

Defences are not permanent solutions but commitments that grow. A wall built to withstand the storms of today must be raised as the sea rises, and every raising protects more property that was built because the previous wall made it seem safe. Each round of investment makes the next one harder to refuse, since abandoning the wall would now mean abandoning more. Engineers can usually design a higher barrier; the deeper difficulty is that the community sheltering behind it has, by then, organised its entire economic life around the expectation that the barrier will hold. In low-lying places the expense eventually outruns what the community can pay, and the decision to leave is then made not by a council in calm weather but by the storm that finally breaks through.

Retreat imposed in that way is the worst version of a policy that might have been tolerable. Households leave in a rush, with property that has lost its value overnight, and they scatter wherever they can find housing, so that the neighbourhood that made the place worth defending dissolves. Planned retreat, by contrast, can be slow. A town can stop permitting new building in the most exposed areas, offer to buy homes when owners choose to sell, and move a school or a clinic inland when it would have needed rebuilding anyway. Spread over decades, such steps let a community move as a community.

None of this means that every shore should be abandoned. Some coasts carry so much population and infrastructure that defending them is plainly worth the cost, and in poor places the money for orderly relocation is often lacking. Nor can retreat simply be ordered from above; people who have lived beside the water for generations have reasons for staying that no compensation formula captures, and a plan that ignores them will fail. The argument is narrower: retreat belongs among the options from the start, weighed openly alongside walls, rather than held back as an admission of failure until it can no longer be chosen at all.

passage: The defence of meritocracy rests on a simple and appealing idea: that positions and rewards should go to those who earn them, through talent and effort, rather than to those born into the right family. Against the background of aristocratic privilege this was a revolutionary thought, and it remains a powerful one. Yet it has been attacked, with increasing force, on the ground that talent and effort are themselves largely matters of luck. No one chooses the abilities they are born with. And the capacity to work hard, to persist through failure and to defer gratification, is shaped by upbringing, health and circumstance in ways that no one controls. If this is so, the critic concludes, nobody deserves the rewards that meritocracy hands out, and the language of merit is a flattering fiction.

The premises of this argument are difficult to deny, but its conclusion moves too fast. It runs together two different claims that a person might make about a reward. One is that she deserves it in a deep moral sense, that the world would be unjust if she did not have it. The other is that she is entitled to it, because she has met the conditions that a fair set of rules laid down in advance. A runner who wins a race under fair conditions is entitled to the prize even if her speed owes much to her genes and her coaching; to take the prize away on the ground that she was lucky would itself be a wrong, because she trained and competed on the understanding that winning would bring it. Entitlement of this kind does not depend on the winner being the author of her own talents. It depends only on the fairness of the rules and her compliance with them.

Seen in this light, a society can reward productive contributions, and honour the expectations its rules create, without pretending that the rewards measure the moral worth of those who receive them. It also leaves open, as it should, the question of whether the rules themselves are fair, including how much inequality of reward they ought to permit. What the luck argument undermines is not the practice of rewarding achievement but a particular story told about it, the story in which the successful have simply earned their place and the unsuccessful have simply failed to earn theirs. That story is corrosive. It encourages the winners to regard their advantages as wholly their own, and it adds to the losers' material disadvantage the further injury of being told that they deserved it. The remedy is not to abolish merit but to hold it more lightly.

passage: The argument for protecting infant industries is older than most of the arguments now made against it, and it is more respectable than its critics often allow. Its premise is that productivity in many industries is learned rather than given. A new steelworks or shipyard in a country without one begins with inexperienced workers, untested managers and suppliers who do not yet know what it needs; it will make costly mistakes for years before it reaches the efficiency of established foreign rivals. If it must meet those rivals at once, it may never survive long enough to learn. A period of protection, on this view, is not a subsidy to inefficiency but an investment in the learning that will eventually remove it.

The argument gains force from a further point. Much of what a pioneering firm learns does not stay inside it. Workers it trains move to competitors, suppliers it develops go on to serve other customers, and the mere demonstration that an industry can work in a given place lowers the risk for those who follow. Over time a cluster of related firms may form around the pioneer, each drawing on skills that the pioneer paid to create. Because the pioneer bears the cost of this learning but captures only part of its benefit, an unaided market will produce too little of it, and there is a case in principle for public support.

The difficulty lies not in the logic but in the ending. Protection is granted on the promise that it is temporary, yet every year it lasts it builds a constituency for its continuation: owners whose profits depend on it, workers whose jobs appear to, and officials whose standing is tied to the industry's survival. Worse, the protection itself weakens the motive to learn. A firm that knows its shelter will be extended whenever it fails to become competitive has little reason to bear the pain of becoming so, and the infant can remain an infant indefinitely, growing larger without growing up. The many cases in which protection outlived any plausible learning period are not accidents of bad administration; they are what the incentives predict.

It follows that the argument stands or falls on whether the exit can be made credible in advance. Protection whose duration is fixed and public, whose renewal depends on measurable progress, and whose beneficiaries are required to compete in some market where the shelter does not reach them, such as export markets, is a different policy from protection granted open-endedly. Export performance is especially revealing, because a firm cannot fake competitiveness in a market it does not control. A protected firm that must also sell abroad, at prices set by rivals it cannot shut out, learns quickly whether it has improved, and so does the government that shelters it. The interesting historical question is therefore not whether successful industrialisers protected their industries, since many did, but whether they attached conditions that forced the protected firms to improve.

None of this makes the conditions easy to impose. Withdrawing support from a large employer that has missed its targets requires a government able to bear the political cost, and the very constituency that protection creates is what makes that cost high. Protection also has victims who are easy to overlook: the firms that must buy the sheltered product at a higher price, and whose own competitiveness suffers as a result. The infant-industry case, then, is best understood not as a general licence but as a demanding bargain, sound in theory and available in practice only to states that can enforce its terms.

passage: A familiar way of thinking about pollution treats it as a simple wrong: one party harms another, and the law should stop the harm or make the harmer pay. An influential argument in economics asks us to look at the situation differently. Suppose the smoke from a small factory soils the washing of a few households nearby. The harm, on this view, is reciprocal: to protect the washing is to restrict the factory, and to protect the factory is to burden the households. If the parties could bargain freely and cheaply, the argument runs, they would arrive at the efficient outcome whoever held the legal right. If the households had the right to clean air, the factory would pay them to tolerate some smoke whenever its gains exceeded their losses; if the factory had the right to emit, the households would pay it to fit a filter whenever the filter cost less than the damage it prevented.

The conclusion is often summarised as a reason for governments to stand aside: define property rights clearly, and private bargaining will do the rest. That reading takes the conditional for the claim. The striking result holds only when bargaining is nearly costless, and the more interesting lesson lies in how rarely that condition is met. A few households and one factory can meet around a table. A city of several million people breathing the exhaust of a million vehicles cannot. Each resident's share of the harm is small, working out who caused how much of it is difficult, and every resident has a reason to let others negotiate and pay while enjoying the cleaner air for nothing. The costs of finding the parties, measuring the damage and enforcing an agreement swamp whatever gains the bargain might bring.

Read in this way, the argument is less a case against regulation than a map of where it is needed. Where the parties are few, the harm is visible and agreements can be checked, private settlement may indeed work better than a rule imposed from outside; the neighbours of a noisy workshop may settle a dispute over evening hours more sensibly than any ordinance could. Where the parties are many and scattered, the same reasoning that praises bargaining in principle explains why it will not happen in practice, and why a tax, a standard or a tradable permit can stand in for a negotiation that no one is able to hold.

None of this makes the assignment of rights a matter of indifference. Even when bargaining would reach the same physical outcome, it matters a great deal who pays whom. A rule that gives the factory the right to pollute leaves the households poorer by the price of their clean air; a rule that gives them the right leaves the factory's owners poorer instead. Efficiency may be blind to that difference. Those who live downwind are not.

passage: Few words are used more freely by restaurant reviewers than 'authentic', and few are applied more selectively. A dish is praised as authentic when it is served in a cramped room, by a cook who speaks the diner's language haltingly, at a price that suggests nobody is getting rich. The same dish, served with tablecloths and a wine list, is suspected of having been tamed. Authenticity, in this usage, is less a property of the food than of the scene around it, and the scene is one that the visiting diner has come to consume.

Consider a hypothetical family that opens a restaurant serving the cooking of its home region in a city several thousand kilometres away. From the start, the cooks make changes. Some ingredients cannot be found and are replaced with local ones; some dishes are too laborious for a kitchen that must turn out fifty plates a night; others are sweetened or softened because the first customers sent them back. Within a generation the menu has become something that exists nowhere else: neither the food of the home region nor the food of the new city, but the food of the people who moved between them.

Purists treat this history as a decline, and they reward the restaurants that seem to have resisted it, the ones with a second menu in the home language that outsiders must know to ask for. Yet even that second menu has passed through the same kitchen, the same suppliers and the same compromises. To call it the real food and the first menu a betrayal is to take one stage of a continuous adaptation and freeze it as the original. More troubling, the judgement is usually made by people with no stake in the tradition, who are in effect asking immigrant cooks to perform their own foreignness for an audience's satisfaction.

None of this means that every adaptation is innocent. Cooks under commercial pressure sometimes strip a cuisine of everything difficult until it is recognisable only by name, and something real is lost when that happens. But the loss is better described as a narrowing of what the cooks themselves are free to make than as a departure from a fixed original. The more useful question to ask of a restaurant is not whether its food matches some imagined source, but whether the people cooking it have the room to cook what they think is good.

passage: For a period, small loans to the poor were spoken of as something close to a cure. The story was compelling: a woman borrows a modest sum, buys a second sewing machine or a stock of vegetables to sell, repays from her profits, borrows again, and climbs by degrees out of poverty. Lenders who reported repayment rates that conventional banks could only envy seemed to prove that the poor were creditworthy, and from creditworthiness it seemed a short step to prosperity. The step proved longer than advertised.

When careful evaluations compared similar communities with and without access to microcredit, they tended to find effects that were real but modest. Some households started or expanded businesses; average incomes and consumption rose little, if at all; and the transformation of lives promised in the brochures was hard to find in the data. It would be easy to read this as a verdict that microcredit failed. That reading, I think, mistakes what was being tested. The original story assumed that most poor people are frustrated entrepreneurs held back only by a lack of capital. Many are not. They run tiny enterprises because steady wage work is unavailable, and given the choice many would take a factory job at a fixed wage over the uncertainties of a market stall.

Seen in this light, the more interesting finding is how borrowers actually used their loans. A good deal of the money went not into enterprises but into managing life's lumpy expenses: a wedding, a hospital bill, school fees due all at once, a new roof before the rains. For households whose incomes arrive irregularly, the ability to turn a stream of small repayments into a single usable sum is genuinely valuable, even if it never shows up as a rise in average income. Microcredit, on this view, is less an engine of growth than a financial service, comparable to the savings and insurance that the better-off take for granted.

This reframing is not a licence for complacency. Where lenders multiply and compete for the same clients, households can take one loan to repay another, and a service that smooths hardship can become a source of it. Nor should the modest average conceal a minority of borrowers, usually those who already ran established businesses, for whom credit made a larger difference. The lesson is not that small loans are worthless but that they should be judged as what they are, and regulated with that in mind, rather than against a promise they were never likely to keep.

passage: Few ideas feel more natural than the distinction between home and work. We leave one for the other in the morning and return in the evening, and much of our moral vocabulary depends on the contrast: home is where we are valued for who we are, work where we are valued for what we produce. Yet for most of recorded history, in most agrarian and artisan societies, the distinction would have puzzled the people who lived in households. The house was where the work was done.

Consider a weaver's dwelling in a pre-industrial town, or a farmstead in the countryside. The looms or the dairy stood beside the hearth, and the people who ate at the table included not only parents and children but apprentices, servants and labourers who lived under the same roof and the same authority. The head of the household was at once father, employer and, in a limited sense, magistrate, answerable to the wider community for the conduct of everyone in his charge. Records of such households often used the word family to mean this whole working unit, and a reader who assumes that it meant blood relatives alone will misread them badly. Children worked as soon as they were able, carding wool or minding animals, and learning a trade was part of growing up in the house rather than something that began when a child left it.

None of this should be romanticised. The working household was a hierarchy, often a harsh one, in which servants could be beaten and wives had little legal standing apart from their husbands. Nor was it universal: the poorest labourers, who owned no tools and rented a single room, had little to bring home but their wages. The point is not that the old arrangement was better, but that it was different in kind, and that the difference matters for how we read later history.

When production moved into workshops, mills and offices, the household did not simply lose its economic role; it acquired a new meaning. Freed of the loom and the dairy, it could be imagined as a private refuge, governed by affection rather than discipline, and this ideal was then projected backwards as if it had always existed. The ideal was real enough for those who could afford it, but it was an ideal, not a description of the past. Laments about the decline of the family often rest on that projection. What changed over these centuries was less the strength of family feeling than the range of tasks the household was expected to perform, and a history that confuses the two will find decline where there was mainly transformation.

passage: Most national histories begin with a land and a people presented as though they had always been there, waiting to become a nation. Kings who reigned many centuries earlier, battles fought for reasons that had nothing to do with any modern state, and poets who wrote in dialects their supposed descendants can barely read are enlisted as the opening chapters of a single story whose last chapter is the present. Rulers who owed allegiance to dynasties spread across several of today's countries, and who would not have recognised the modern map, are recast as founders. The past is read backwards from its outcome and then retold forwards as if the outcome had been its purpose all along.

Critics call this anachronism, and on the main charge they are right. But the criticism is often pressed further than it can go, into the claim that because nations are modern creations, the materials of national history are simply invented. That does not follow. Languages, forms of worship, routes of trade and shared songs long predated modern states, and they plainly did shape which communities later found it easy, and which found it hard, to imagine themselves as one. The national historian's mistake is not to notice these continuities. It is to arrange them as stages on the way to an end that was fixed in advance.

The distinction matters because the arrangement has consequences. If the nation is the hero of the story, then whatever the past contained that does not fit the hero's career must be either left out or cast as a failure of loyalty. Regions that resisted unification, communities whose ties ran across the eventual border, rival projects that might have produced a different state or several smaller ones: all of these become obstacles overcome rather than possibilities that once existed and were, for a time, taken seriously by the people who lived among them. A province that held out for its own arrangements appears only as a delay, and a language that lost out to the standard tongue appears, if at all, as a quaint survival. The coherence of the story is purchased by narrowing its cast.

A better history would keep the continuities and restore the alternatives. It would ask what other political communities were possible at each point, what the people of the time thought they were choosing between, and why this one prevailed, treating the result as an outcome to be explained rather than a destiny to be celebrated. Such a history may make for less stirring lessons in school. It is also far less likely to make citizens strangers to whole regions and peoples of their own past.
